description.narrative: BeletWeyne district is experiencing a severe humanitarian crisis marked by escalating food insecurity. Extensive flooding has submerged over 4,990 hectares of farmland, devastating local agriculture. This environmental disaster, coupled with prolonged dry spells,displacement, and soaring food prices, has left many households unable to meet their basic food needs, necessitating urgent humanitarian intervention. In response, the project targets 1,977 vulnerable households—approximately 11,862 individuals—including 5,955 internally displaced persons (IDPs), 54% women-headed households, and 480 persons with disabilities. These beneficiaries are located across 13 priority sites consisting of six IDP settlements and seven host villages distributed across northern, eastern, and southernparts of the district. The intervention is designed to provide lifesaving unconditional cash transfers (UCT) valued at $55 per household per month for three months, totaling $326,205. The UCTs aim to enhance immediate access to food by enabling households to purchase essential items, offering recipients the autonomy to address their specific needs while revitalizing local markets. The projectwill provide emergency agricultural inputs worth $45 each to 500 vulnerable households with access to arable land. These inputs include climate-resilient, short-cycle seeds to facilitate the production of early-maturing crops, extending food availability beyond the immediate relief phase and improving household dietary diversity. Beneficiaries will also receive training on climate-smart agricultural practices, including soil conservation and water management techniques, aimed at enhancing productivity and building resilience to future environmental shocks. This dual approach—addressing both immediate consumption gaps and supporting local food production ensures a more holistic response to the crisis. Beneficiary selection follows a rigorous vulnerability-based targeting process, prioritizing households facing multiple risk factors, suchas displacement, female headship, disability, and limited livelihood options. This ensures that resources reach those most in need, maximizing the intervention’s impact. Cash transfers will be delivered primarily through secure mobile money platforms, facilitating safe, timely, and efficient distribution. In areas with limited mobile network coverage, alternative cash delivery mechanisms will be utilized with robust monitoring to ensure transparency and accountability. Agricultural inputs will be distributed alongside technical guidance and support to optimize crop yields and sustainability. Oxfam will leverage its existing programs in Belet Weyne, funded by the Dutch Relief Alliance and AiCS, to integrate this intervention within a broader multi-sectoral framework. Active participation in the Area-Based Coordination (ABC) platform will enhance collaboration with local authorities, humanitarian actors, and community stakeholders, ensuring a harmonized, locally informed, and cost-effective response. The project’s protection-sensitive design also incorporates measures to mitigate gender-based violence risks and ensure the dignity and safety of all beneficiaries, particularly women and persons with disabilities. This intervention is fully alignedwith theSHF Standard Allocation 1 –2025 Strategy and the priorities outlined in the Food Security Cluster and the 2025 HumanitarianResponse Plan. By addressing immediate food access through cash transfers and supporting household food production with agriculturalinputs and capacity building, the project tackles both urgent humanitarian needs and longer-term resilience building.

participating-org.narrative: In 2004 Oxfam Novib set up a Liaison Office in Nairobi, Kenya in order to support the Strengthening Somali Civil Society Program, at the request of the EU. This request was based on Oxfam Novib's work in Somalia to date, but intended to be more widely directed atthe entire civil society sector and the specific context in which it is operating in a post-conflict country. The program started with consulting local organisations in Somalia and Somaliland to get a complete picture of the sectors and regions where they are active, the challenges they face and the relationship between civil society, local political structures and the private sector. A program was then developed to strengthen the institutional development of Oxfam Novib's partners and those of other Oxfams, as well as a range of new NGOs. In the first year local consultants were trained in Somalia. They were then seconded to civil society organisations to build their capacity in financial and organisational management. Furthermore, workshops were organised on specific themes suchas human rights and the role of civil society in the Somali context. The Liaison Office is now going to support the expansion of the program, focussing on strengthening both organisation and project management, while facilitating more training in the fields of civic education, governance, human rights and women's rights, HIV and AIDS and child protection. Over the years, the Somalia Country Office has expanded its intervention on short term humanitarian response as well as development development interventions. In 2015/2016, a decision was reached to move the Country Programme operation, which was largely in Nairobi, from Nairobi to Hargeisa. The country office has a small office in Nairobi , Kenya and large operations office in Hargeisa, Somaliland.
